newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil aims to ban widespread child labor.
newsitem.headline: Brazil aims to ban widespread child labor.

text.p: President Fernando Henrique Cardoso on Thursday sent a bill to Congress to ban child labour and take 3.5 million Brazilian children out of coal factories and sugar cane fields and put them back into school.

In a bid to beef up a much-touted plan to end the widespread use of child workers, Cardoso asked Congress to give quick approval to the constitutional amendment that would "ban definitively" the employment of children up to age 14.

"We must fight the exploitation of children and adolescents," he said at a ceremony in Brasilia's Presidential Palace attended by 200 child workers from across the country. Jose Carlos Bezerra, a 16-year-old sugar cane cutter, and 13-year-old Debora Alves da Silva, a cotton picker, handed Cardoso a symbolic machete at the ceremony.
The children delivered a petition demanding "more radical" actions in the fight against child labour, including more police inspection and more severe penalties for employers.

In September the government took the first step toward tackling child labour by offering to pay about $25 a month to parents who put their children back in school. It also signed a joint declaration with labour unions, pressure groups, churches and the states to cooperate in the fight against the employment of children under the age of 14.

The government's IBGE statistics office puts the number of under-14s in work at about 3.5 million out of Brazil's total population of 160 million. But other independent bodies say as many as 7.5 million young Brazilians are forced by their impoverished parents to contribute to the family income.

The United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) and the International Labour Organisation (ILO) said this month they would step up their international efforts to force governments to implement global labour standards. The ILO said 73 million children between the ages of 10 and 14 work worldwide -- 13 percent of all children in that age group.
According to the U.N., about 17 percent of Latin American children work, with the proportion in Brazil being one of the highest at 32 percent.

Brazil's National Confederation of Agricultural Workers (CONTAG) on Thursday suggested firms that take on child workers should be banned from exporting their products and should be denied access to federal loans.
